title: 125. Quantitative Relationships & Measurement: Dimensional Consistency of Equations
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Dimensional Consistency of a Basic Kinematic Equation
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether the equation \(v=\frac{d}{t}\) is dimensionally consistent.
questions.question: Let \(v\) have SI unit \(\text{m/s}\), \(d\) have SI unit \(\text{m}\), and nonzero \(t\) have SI unit \(\text{s}\). Which statement about \(v=\frac{d}{t}\) is correct?
questions.explanation: Speed has dimension \(LT^{-1}\). Dividing a length by a time has the same dimension, so the equation is consistent. Calling it inconsistent overlooks the time in the denominator.
questions.hint: Compare the dimension of each term on both sides.

questions.concept: Dimensional Consistency of a Displacement Equation
questions.question: Let \(s\) be a displacement, \(v\) a speed, \(a\) an acceleration, and \(t\) a time. Is \(s=vt+\frac{1}{2}at^2\) dimensionally consistent?
questions.explanation: Both \(vt\) and \(\frac{1}{2}at^2\) have dimension \(L\), matching displacement. The alternative rejects an equation whose terms all have the same dimension.
questions.hint: Replace each physical quantity by its mass, length, and time dimensions.

questions.concept: Dimensional Consistency of Newton's Second Law
questions.question: Let \(F\) be force, \(m\) mass, and \(a\) acceleration. Is \(F=ma\) dimensionally consistent?
questions.explanation: Force has dimension \(MLT^{-2}\). The product of mass and acceleration has the same dimension, so \(F=ma\) is consistent. The alternative incorrectly rejects this match.
questions.hint: Replace each physical quantity by its mass, length, and time dimensions.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which of two kinematic equations is dimensionally inconsistent.
questions.question: Let \(v\) be speed, \(a\) acceleration, and nonzero \(t\) time. Which equation is dimensionally inconsistent?
questions.explanation: The product \(at\) has dimension \(LT^{-1}\), matching speed. The quotient \(\frac{a}{t}\) has dimension \(LT^{-3}\), so only the quotient equation is inconsistent.
questions.hint: Compare the dimension of each term on both sides.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which equation for pressure is dimensionally inconsistent.
questions.question: Let \(P\) be pressure, \(F\) force, and nonzero \(A\) area. Which equation is dimensionally inconsistent?
questions.explanation: Pressure has dimension \(ML^{-1}T^{-2}\), obtained from force divided by area. The product \(FA\) has dimension \(ML^3T^{-2}\), so it is inconsistent with pressure.
questions.hint: Replace each physical quantity by its mass, length, and time dimensions.

questions.learningObjective: Use dimensions to distinguish a quotient equation from a product equation for acceleration.
questions.question: Let \(a\) be acceleration, \(\Delta v\) a change in velocity, and nonzero \(\Delta t\) a time interval. Which equation is dimensionally consistent?
questions.explanation: Velocity has dimension \(LT^{-1}\), and time has dimension \(T\). Their quotient has dimension \(LT^{-2}\), matching acceleration. Their product has dimension \(L\), matching displacement rather than acceleration.
questions.hint: Compare the dimension of each term on both sides.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the dimensions of the coefficient \(\frac{1}{2}\) in a kinematic equation.
questions.question: Let \(x\) be displacement, \(v_0\) initial velocity, \(a\) acceleration, and \(t\) time. In \(x=v_0t+\frac{1}{2}at^2\), what units must the coefficient \(\frac{1}{2}\) have?
questions.explanation: Both \(v_0t\) and \(at^2\) have dimension \(L\). Their coefficient must be dimensionless to preserve that dimension. Giving \(\frac{1}{2}\) a length unit would make the acceleration term have dimension \(L^2\).
questions.hint: Compare the dimension of each term on both sides.

questions.concept: Dimensions in the Period of a Simple Pendulum
questions.learningObjective: Determine the dimension of the period \(T\) in \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}\).
questions.question: Let \(l\) have dimension length and positive \(g\) have dimension acceleration. In \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}\), what is the dimension of \(T\)?
questions.explanation: The quotient \(\frac{l}{g}\) has dimension \(T^2\). Its square root has dimension \(T\); the factor \(2\pi\) is dimensionless. Length is therefore not the dimension of the result.
questions.hint: Replace each physical quantity by its mass, length, and time dimensions.

questions.concept: Identifying an Expression with a Given SI Unit
questions.learningObjective: Identify which expression related to \(v^2=v_0^2+2ax\) has SI unit \(\frac{\text{m}^2}{\text{s}^2}\).
questions.question: Let \(v\) and \(v_0\) be velocities, \(a\) acceleration, and \(x\) displacement. For the equation \(v^2=v_0^2+2ax\), which of the following expressions has SI unit \(\frac{\text{m}^2}{\text{s}^2}\)?
questions.explanation: The product \(2ax\) has dimension \(L^2T^{-2}\), represented by SI unit \(\frac{\text{m}^2}{\text{s}^2}\). The expression \(v_0\) has dimension \(LT^{-1}\), so it does not match the squared-velocity unit.
questions.hint: A numerical coefficient must preserve the dimension of its term.

questions.learningObjective: Use dimensions to identify a consistent equation for momentum.
questions.question: Momentum \(p\) has dimension \(MLT^{-1}\). Let \(m\) be mass and \(v\) velocity. Which equation is dimensionally consistent?
questions.explanation: Momentum has dimension \(MLT^{-1}\). The product \(mv\) has this dimension, whereas \(\frac{m}{v}\) has dimension \(ML^{-1}T\).
questions.hint: Compare the dimension of each term on both sides.
